name: Baratoplata from Crackhead Control
description: Master the Baratoplata from Crackhead Control. Complete guide to this 10th Planet shoulder lock with setup mechanics, finishing details, and safety protocols.
overview:
The Baratoplata from Crackhead Control is a specialized shoulder lock that exploits the unique leg positioning of the 10th Planet rubber guard system to generate devastating rotational force on the opponent's shoulder joint. From Crackhead Control, the bottom player already has their shin positioned across the back of the opponent's neck with deep posture control established, making this one of the most mechanically efficient setups for the baratoplata available in modern grappling. The existing arm isolation from the overhook grip and compressed posture means the attacking player can transition directly into the figure-four threading without the extensive setup work required from less dominant positions.

The submission works by threading the attacking arm underneath the opponent's trapped arm and connecting to the controlling leg, creating a figure-four configuration that uses hip extension to drive internal rotation of the shoulder beyond its anatomical limits. The key mechanical advantage of this entry is that Crackhead Control already provides two of the three prerequisites for the baratoplata: posture control and arm isolation. The attacker only needs to complete the figure-four connection and apply rotational pressure, reducing the setup time and defensive windows compared to entries from open guard or half guard.

What makes this variation particularly dangerous at the competitive level is the deceptive nature of the attack within the Crackhead Control attack chain. Opponents defending against Crackhead Control typically focus on preventing the more common gogoplata or omoplata threats, leaving the baratoplata as a secondary attack that catches defenders off-guard. The leg-assisted mechanics generate significantly more torque than arm-only shoulder locks like the americana or kimura, making this a genuinely threatening submission even against larger or stronger opponents. The shoulder joint can reach structural failure before adequate pain signals register, demanding exceptional care during training.

8-12 weeks minimum, potential for chronic instability

Never use competition speed during training rolls

Beginners should only practice entry mechanics, not finishing pressure

variations_and_setups.description: From established crackhead control with overhook grip, release the overhook and immediately thread the arm underneath the opponent's trapped arm while maintaining shin pressure across the neck. The overhook-to-thread transition is the highest percentage entry because the arm is already positioned near the threading path.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When you have a solid crackhead control with the opponent's posture fully broken and the overhook grip firmly established on the far arm

variations_and_setups.description: Initiate the gogoplata setup by angling the shin toward the opponent's throat, forcing them to tuck their chin and drive their arm deeper to defend. When their arm commits to the chin defense, abandon the gogoplata angle and immediately thread for the baratoplata. The defensive arm position from gogoplata defense creates an ideal baratoplata entry angle.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the opponent has strong chin defense and repeatedly blocks gogoplata attempts from crackhead control

variations_and_setups.variation_name: Late-Stage Entry from Partial Posture Recovery
variations_and_setups.description: When the opponent begins posturing up and the crackhead control is weakening, use the remaining leg pressure to trap one arm while threading the figure-four before full posture recovery. This requires faster execution and relies on catching the arm during the transition between compressed and postured positions.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When crackhead control is deteriorating and the opponent is partially posturing but one arm remains trapped by your leg configuration

attacker.name: from Crackhead Control Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack with the Baratoplata from Crackhead Control. Step-by-step finishing mechanics, grip threading, and hip extension details for this 10th Planet shoulder lock.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the Baratoplata from Crackhead Control requires understanding the unique advantages this rubber guard position provides for shoulder lock mechanics. The shin-across-neck control already breaks the opponent's posture and partially isolates the target arm, eliminating the two most difficult prerequisites for shoulder lock submissions. Your primary task as the attacker is recognizing when the arm isolation is sufficient to abandon the overhook and commit to the figure-four threading sequence. The transition from control grip to submission grip is the critical moment where most attacks succeed or fail, and the timing must account for the opponent's defensive reactions to the grip change. Mastering the hip angle adjustment and controlled extension that generates the finishing torque transforms this from a positional curiosity into a legitimate competition weapon.
key_principles: Maintain shin pressure across the opponent's neck throughout the entire submission sequence to prevent posture recovery during the threading transition
Thread the attacking arm smoothly in one continuous motion rather than reaching in stages, which telegraphs the attack and allows defensive arm extraction
Use hip extension as the primary force generator for the finish rather than arm pulling, which provides superior leverage and reduces energy expenditure
Angle your hips away from the trapped arm side before applying pressure to align rotational force through the shoulder's weakest plane of motion
Keep the figure-four connection tight with zero slack between your forearm and shin to prevent the opponent from rotating their elbow and relieving pressure
Apply finishing pressure gradually over 5-7 seconds to allow adequate time for the training partner to recognize and respond to the submission
setup_requirements: Established crackhead control with shin positioned across the back of the opponent's neck and posture fully broken
Overhook grip controlling the opponent's far arm with the elbow trapped between your leg and their body
Opponent's head driven below your chest level with no space for posture recovery
Opposite leg active and positioned to maintain balance during the hip angle adjustment and finishing extension
Clear identification that the target arm is sufficiently isolated and cannot be easily extracted before committing to the thread

execution_steps.description: Confirm your shin is firmly across the back of the opponent's neck with the overhook controlling their far arm. Their posture should be completely broken with their head below your chest. Test the arm isolation by briefly increasing overhook pressure - if the arm stays trapped, proceed with the submission.

execution_steps.action: Release overhook and initiate arm thread
execution_steps.description: Release the overhook grip and immediately begin threading your attacking arm underneath the opponent's trapped arm. Your hand passes between their forearm and your controlling shin, traveling from the outside of their arm to the inside. Maintain strong shin pressure throughout to compensate for the momentary loss of the overhook grip.
execution_steps.timing: 1-2 seconds, must be smooth and continuous

execution_steps.description: After threading your arm through, grab your own shin or ankle on the controlling leg to close the figure-four loop around the opponent's arm. The opponent's elbow should be positioned at the center of the loop acting as the fulcrum point for the rotational leverage. Ensure there is no slack in the connection between your forearm grip and shin.

execution_steps.action: Adjust hip angle for optimal leverage
execution_steps.description: Shift your hips approximately 30 degrees away from the trapped arm side to align the rotational force vector directly through the shoulder joint's weakest plane of motion. This angle change is critical for generating effective internal rotation rather than simple compression. Keep your opposite leg posted for balance during the adjustment.

Initiate the finishing sequence by extending your hips forward while simultaneously pulling the figure-four connection toward your chest. This dual action creates internal rotation of the opponent's shoulder that bypasses their normal rotator cuff resistance. Begin slowly to establish the rotational path before increasing pressure.

execution_steps.action: Drive hip extension for maximum torque
execution_steps.description: Continue driving your hips upward and forward while maintaining the tight figure-four connection, generating compound rotational torque on the shoulder. The combination of hip extension and arm pull creates force the opponent cannot resist through muscular strength alone. Monitor the opponent's body language and tap signals throughout the pressure application.

execution_steps.action: Complete finish or release on tap
execution_steps.description: Maintain controlled pressure until the opponent taps or verbally submits. Release immediately upon any tap signal by stopping all hip extension, releasing the figure-four grip, and allowing the opponent to safely extract their arm. If the opponent does not tap and their arm reaches end range of motion, hold steady pressure without increasing force and verbally confirm they are okay.
execution_steps.timing: Immediate release upon tap, 1-2 seconds to fully disengage

common_counters.your_response: If the opponent begins posturing during the threading, abort the baratoplata and re-establish the overhook for crackhead control. Alternatively, use the remaining leg pressure to transition to a gogoplata attempt as they posture into the shin.

common_counters.counter: Arm straightening to prevent figure-four closure
common_counters.your_response: When the opponent straightens their trapped arm, increase shin pressure to keep them compressed while using your free hand to bend their elbow by pushing on their wrist. If the arm stays straight, transition to an omoplata angle using the existing leg position.

common_counters.counter: Elbow rotation to relieve shoulder pressure
common_counters.your_response: Tighten the figure-four connection by pulling your shin closer to your forearm, eliminating the space needed for elbow rotation. Simultaneously increase hip extension to accelerate the finish before they can complete the rotation.

common_counters.counter: Explosive bridge and stack to collapse guard
common_counters.your_response: If the opponent bridges forward to stack you, use the momentum to angle further onto your shoulder and increase the rotational leverage. The bridge actually assists the shoulder lock if you maintain the figure-four connection and hip angle.

common_counters.counter: Full-body roll toward trapped arm side
common_counters.your_response: Follow the roll while maintaining the figure-four and use the rotational momentum to accelerate the finish. The roll typically worsens their position as it drives additional internal rotation through the shoulder joint.

common_errors.error: Releasing shin pressure during the arm threading transition
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recovers posture and extracts their arm, escaping crackhead control entirely and resetting to closed guard or standing
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant downward shin pressure across the neck throughout the threading sequence, using your opposite leg to reinforce control if needed

common_errors.error: Threading the arm too slowly or in multiple attempts
common_errors.consequence: Telegraphs the submission attempt, giving the opponent time to straighten their arm and deny the figure-four or begin postural defense
common_errors.correction: Commit to a single smooth threading motion once you decide to attack, treating the overhook release and arm thread as one continuous action

common_errors.error: Leaving slack in the figure-four connection between forearm and shin
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can rotate their elbow within the loop to relieve rotational pressure on the shoulder, converting the submission into a neutral grip fight
common_errors.correction: Pull the shin-forearm connection as tight as possible before initiating hip extension, eliminating all dead space in the figure-four

common_errors.error: Attempting to finish with arm strength instead of hip extension
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient torque to overcome the opponent's shoulder resistance, rapid grip fatigue, and loss of the submission position within 10-15 seconds
common_errors.correction: Use hip extension as the primary force generator, keeping arms in a fixed figure-four position while the hips drive the rotational pressure

common_errors.error: Failing to angle hips away from the trapped arm before applying pressure
common_errors.consequence: Rotational force is misaligned with the shoulder's vulnerable axis, reducing effective torque by approximately 40% and allowing muscular resistance to stall the finish
common_errors.correction: Shift hips 30 degrees away from the trapped arm side before beginning any finishing pressure to align force with the shoulder's weakest rotational plane

common_errors.error: Applying finishing pressure explosively rather than gradually
common_errors.consequence: Risk of severe shoulder injury including rotator cuff tear or dislocation, as the joint can fail structurally before pain signals register
common_errors.correction: Apply pressure over a minimum of 5-7 seconds with gradual increase, monitoring the opponent's tap signals and body language throughout

training_progressions.focus: Hip angle adjustment and controlled extension

Partner taps at first sign of shoulder pressure. Focus on using hips rather than arms and on controlled application speed.

Run the full sequence from crackhead control through finish with the partner providing increasing levels of resistance. Partner defends with posture recovery, arm straightening, and elbow rotation at 50-75% effort. Attacker must adjust to each defense while maintaining control throughout.

knowledge_assessment.question: What anatomical structures does the Baratoplata from Crackhead Control primarily attack?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The baratoplata primarily attacks the shoulder joint through forced internal rotation, targeting the rotator cuff muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis) and the glenohumeral ligaments. The figure-four configuration creates rotational torque that stresses the shoulder capsule and can cause tears to the labrum or rotator cuff tendons when applied with force. The compound nature of the leg-assisted leverage makes it particularly dangerous because the force generation exceeds what arm-only shoulder locks produce.

knowledge_assessment.question: What distinguishes the Crackhead Control entry for the baratoplata from setups in other positions?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Crackhead Control provides pre-existing posture control and arm isolation that other setups lack. The shin across the back of the neck keeps the opponent compressed, and the overhook naturally positions the target arm for the figure-four threading. This eliminates two of the three major setup steps required from other positions - posture breaking and arm isolation - making the entry significantly more efficient with a smaller defensive window for the opponent to exploit.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the point of no escape for the defender during this submission?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The point of no escape occurs when the figure-four connection between the attacking arm and controlling leg is fully closed with no slack, and the attacker begins hip extension with proper hip angle. Once the closed loop is complete around the trapped arm with the attacker's hips angled away, the defender cannot extract their arm without the attacker releasing the connection. Defensive efforts must address the submission before the figure-four closes, as post-connection defenses rely on disrupting the hip angle rather than escaping the arm trap.

knowledge_assessment.question: How should you adjust finishing pressure against an opponent with unusually flexible shoulders?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Against flexible opponents, extend the hip drive further while simultaneously pulling the figure-four connection closer to your own centerline, increasing the total rotational arc. You may also need to steepen the hip angle beyond the standard 30 degrees to access a more vulnerable rotation plane. The key indicator is feeling the shoulder reach its end range of motion. Continue applying slow, steady pressure past the initial flexibility range rather than abandoning the submission. Flexible opponents still have a structural limit, it simply requires more rotation to reach.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the critical safety protocols when training the Baratoplata from Crackhead Control?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Apply finishing pressure over a minimum of 5-7 seconds, never explosively. The shoulder joint can sustain structural damage including rotator cuff tears and labrum damage before the opponent feels sufficient pain to tap. Release immediately upon any tap signal including verbal, hand tap, or foot tap on any surface. During drilling, stop at the first sign of shoulder resistance rather than pushing through. Partners with prior shoulder injuries should avoid this technique entirely, and beginners should practice only the entry and figure-four mechanics without applying any finishing pressure.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the most common finishing errors that allow the opponent to escape the baratoplata?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The three most common finishing errors are: first, failing to angle the hips away from the trapped arm before applying pressure, which reduces rotational leverage by approximately 40 percent; second, leaving slack in the figure-four connection between forearm and shin, which gives the opponent space to rotate their elbow and relieve pressure; and third, attempting to finish with arm strength alone rather than using hip extension as the primary force generator, which causes rapid fatigue and insufficient torque. Each error independently can convert a locked submission into an escape opportunity.

knowledge_assessment.question: What grip adjustments should you make during the finish if the opponent begins active defense?
knowledge_assessment.answer: If the opponent attempts to straighten their trapped arm, tighten the figure-four by pulling your shin closer to your forearm and increase shin pressure across the neck to maintain compression. If they try to posture up, reinforce the crackhead control leg position before continuing the finish. If they attempt to roll toward the trapped arm side, follow their rotation while maintaining the figure-four connection and use the momentum to accelerate the submission. Each defensive response has a corresponding adjustment that maintains or increases submission pressure rather than requiring a restart.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does the baratoplata from Crackhead Control integrate into a competition submission strategy?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The baratoplata functions as a secondary threat within the crackhead control attack chain, complementing the primary gogoplata threat. In competition, establish the gogoplata angle first to force chin-tucking and arm-defensive reactions that expose the arm for baratoplata threading. This creates a genuine dilemma where defending one submission opens the other. The surprise factor is significant at all competitive levels because most practitioners drill gogoplata defenses extensively but have limited baratoplata defense experience, making it an effective weapon for catching prepared opponents.

knowledge_assessment.question: How should you release the Baratoplata from Crackhead Control after your training partner taps?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Upon any tap signal, immediately stop all hip extension and forward pressure on the shoulder. Release the figure-four grip by letting go of your shin, then unwrap the controlling leg from behind the opponent's neck. Lower your hips to remove all rotational force from the shoulder before allowing your partner to extract their arm at their own pace. Check that they have full shoulder mobility and no pain before resuming training. Never maintain any pressure while releasing, as the shoulder is at its most vulnerable at end range of motion.

defender.name: from Crackhead Control Defender
defender.description: Learn to defend against the Baratoplata from Crackhead Control. Recognition cues, prevention timing, emergency escapes, and safe tapping protocols for this shoulder lock.
defender.overview: Defending against the Baratoplata from Crackhead Control requires understanding the specific windows of opportunity within the attacker's setup sequence where defensive actions are most effective. The most critical defensive principle is prevention over escape: stopping the figure-four from closing is exponentially easier than escaping once it is established. Defenders must recognize that crackhead control already places them at a significant positional disadvantage, and the baratoplata represents an escalation from a bad position to a submission-danger position. The transition moment when the attacker releases their overhook to begin threading is both the most dangerous moment and the best defensive opportunity. Recognizing this grip change instantly and responding with posture recovery or arm extraction determines whether you face a submission or successfully escape to a safer guard position.
key_principles: Prevention is dramatically more effective than escape - address the submission before the figure-four closes rather than attempting to escape after it locks
The overhook release is your primary recognition cue and defensive trigger - respond immediately when you feel the grip change from overhook to threading attempt
Arm straightening is your most reliable defensive tool - extending the trapped arm fully prevents the figure-four from closing around the elbow
Posture recovery during the threading transition exploits the momentary weakness created when the attacker abandons their overhook control grip
If the figure-four closes, tap early rather than attempting heroic late-stage escapes - the shoulder joint can fail structurally before you feel adequate pain
Use the attacker's commitment to the baratoplata as an opportunity to escape crackhead control entirely through explosive posture recovery
recognition_cues: The attacker releases their overhook grip while maintaining shin pressure across your neck, indicating they are transitioning from control to submission
You feel an arm sliding underneath your trapped arm between your forearm and the attacker's controlling shin
The attacker's hip angle begins shifting away from your trapped arm side as they position for the rotational finish
The attacker's free hand reaches toward their own shin or ankle, indicating they are attempting to close the figure-four connection
You feel increasing rotational pressure on your shoulder joint after a period of standard crackhead control compression

defensive_options.action: Explosive posture recovery during overhook release
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately when you feel the attacker release their overhook grip to begin the arm threading sequence
defensive_options.if_successful: Break through crackhead control entirely and reset to closed guard where the submission threat is eliminated
defensive_options.risk: If the attacker maintains sufficient shin pressure during your posture attempt, you may remain in crackhead control and have wasted energy

defensive_options.action: Arm straightening to prevent figure-four closure
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you feel the attacker's arm beginning to thread underneath your trapped arm
defensive_options.if_successful: Deny the figure-four connection and force the attacker to either re-establish the overhook or attempt a different submission
defensive_options.risk: Straightening the arm while maintaining it in the crackhead control area keeps you in a defensive position with other submission threats still active

defensive_options.action: Elbow drive to hip with full-body rotation
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the figure-four is partially established but not yet tight, as a last-resort prevention before full lock
defensive_options.if_successful: Extract the arm from the partially formed figure-four and return to standard crackhead control defensive posture
defensive_options.risk: If the figure-four is already tight, this motion can accelerate the shoulder rotation and worsen the submission

defensive_options.action: Forward stack and pressure to collapse guard
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker has committed to the baratoplata but has not yet applied strong hip extension
defensive_options.if_successful: Weight pressure disrupts the attacker's hip angle and may collapse the rubber guard position entirely
defensive_options.risk: Driving forward can inadvertently increase shoulder rotation if the attacker maintains the figure-four and adjusts angle

escape_paths: Explosive posture recovery through the threading window when the attacker releases the overhook, driving head and shoulders backward to break through crackhead control to closed guard
Arm straightening and extraction by fully extending the trapped arm and pulling the elbow toward your hip before the figure-four can close around the bent elbow
Forward stacking pressure to collapse the rubber guard structure and force the attacker to release leg control to defend the stack

favorable_outcomes.how: Capitalize on the attacker's overhook release during the baratoplata setup by explosively posturing up and extracting your arm, breaking through crackhead control to reset in closed guard where the immediate submission threat is eliminated

common_errors.error: Waiting to defend until the figure-four is already locked
common_errors.consequence: Once the figure-four closes tight with the attacker's hips angled, defensive options are essentially exhausted and the submission will likely finish
common_errors.correction: Respond to the overhook release or arm threading immediately rather than waiting to assess the threat level - early action prevents the submission while late action only delays it

common_errors.error: Attempting to muscle out of the submission by externally rotating the shoulder
common_errors.consequence: Fighting the rotational pressure with opposing muscle force accelerates fatigue and can cause injury if the joint reaches its limit during the muscular effort
common_errors.correction: Use skeletal structure rather than muscle to defend - straighten the arm to change the geometry rather than trying to rotate against the figure-four leverage

common_errors.error: Ignoring the baratoplata setup while focusing on gogoplata defense
common_errors.consequence: The attacker threads the figure-four unopposed while you defend against a gogoplata that is not actually being attempted, resulting in a locked submission
common_errors.correction: Learn to distinguish between gogoplata setups (shin angling toward throat) and baratoplata setups (overhook release and arm threading) to apply the correct defensive response

common_errors.error: Refusing to tap once the figure-four is locked and hip extension begins
common_errors.consequence: The shoulder joint can sustain structural damage including rotator cuff tears, labrum tears, or dislocation within 1-2 seconds of reaching end range under the compound leg-assisted leverage
common_errors.correction: Tap immediately when you feel the rotational pressure engage your shoulder. The baratoplata develops force faster than arm-only shoulder locks and the damage window between discomfort and structural failure is very narrow

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you recognize that a Baratoplata from Crackhead Control is being set up rather than another attack?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary recognition cue is feeling the attacker release their overhook grip while maintaining shin pressure across your neck. In standard crackhead control, the overhook is maintained for sweeps and gogoplata setups, so releasing it while keeping leg pressure signals a baratoplata attempt. You will then feel an arm threading underneath your trapped arm between your forearm and the attacker's shin. The key distinction from gogoplata setup is that gogoplata involves the shin angling toward your throat, while baratoplata involves the overhook hand moving underneath your arm.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the safest way to tap when caught in the Baratoplata from Crackhead Control?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Tap immediately when you feel rotational pressure beginning in your shoulder, before the pain becomes significant. Use your free hand to tap rapidly on the opponent's body or the mat where they can see or feel it. If your free hand is restricted, say the word tap loudly and clearly. You can also tap with your feet on the mat. The critical principle is to tap early rather than late - the shoulder joint can sustain permanent structural damage including rotator cuff tears and dislocation in the 1-2 seconds between initial pressure and joint failure under the compound leg-assisted leverage.

knowledge_assessment.question: What defensive options are available at each stage of the baratoplata setup?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Before the arm thread begins: posture aggressively to break crackhead control entirely, exploiting the momentary weakness from the overhook release. During the arm thread: immediately straighten your trapped arm fully and pull the elbow toward your hip to prevent the figure-four from closing. After figure-four connection but before hip extension: attempt explosive bridge toward the trapped arm side while driving your elbow to your hip to create space in the loop. Once hip extension begins with proper angle: tap immediately, as effective defensive options are exhausted at this point.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the single most important defensive action to prevent the baratoplata from finishing?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Preventing the figure-four from closing is the decisive defensive moment. When you feel the attacker threading their arm underneath yours, immediately extend your trapped arm straight and drive your elbow toward your own hip. This changes the geometry from a bent-arm position that allows the figure-four to close into a straight-arm configuration that prevents the loop from completing around your elbow. If you can maintain the straight arm for 3-5 seconds, the attacker will typically abandon the baratoplata and return to other crackhead control attacks, giving you a reset without position loss.

knowledge_assessment.question: How can you exploit the opponent's baratoplata attempt to improve your own position?
knowledge_assessment.answer: When the attacker releases their overhook to initiate the baratoplata threading, this momentarily weakens their overall crackhead control by removing one of the two primary control mechanisms. Use this 1-2 second window to explosively posture up, driving your head and shoulders backward while simultaneously pulling your trapped arm free. If successful, you break through crackhead control to closed guard or even beyond. The key is recognizing the grip release as a defensive opportunity rather than purely a threat - the brief period with neither overhook control nor completed figure-four is your best escape window from the entire crackhead control position.

Critically, practice recognizing when the submission is past the point of effective defense and tapping immediately. Build the habit of early tapping under compound shoulder lock pressure.

training_progressions.description: Start in crackhead control with the attacker free to attempt any submission including the baratoplata. Defender works all available escapes and defensive options against unpredictable attacks. Develops the ability to distinguish between different submission threats and apply the correct defensive response in real time.
